title: Environmental Sensor Mapping, Calibration and Spatial Gradients

content.overview: Controlled rooms are not environmentally uniform. Canopy height, lamp position, walls, irrigation zones and airflow create gradients that a single wall sensor can miss, so advanced control starts with representative measurement.

vocabulary.definition: A systematic environmental difference across positions within a room or canopy.
Comparison and adjustment of a sensor against a known reference or validated standard.
A measurement strategy intended to describe the conditions actually experienced by the crop.

sections.title: One sensor cannot describe a complex canopy
sections.body: Temperature and humidity can differ vertically and horizontally. Mapping should include canopy-level and problem-prone positions instead of relying only on controller placement.

sections.title: Sensor quality is part of control quality
sections.body: Drift, shielding, response time and radiant heating can distort readings. Calibration checks and colocated comparisons help separate real environmental change from sensor error.

sections.title: Maps should drive hypotheses
sections.body: Repeated hot, humid or stagnant zones should trigger investigation of airflow, heat sources, crop density or irrigation rather than arbitrary setpoint changes.

workedExamples: If a wall sensor reads acceptable humidity while interior canopy probes remain higher, treat the canopy measurements as evidence of a spatial problem rather than averaging the issue away.
If one sensor consistently differs from colocated peers, verify calibration before redesigning the HVAC schedule.
commonMistakes: Mounting every sensor outside the crop zone.
Treating controller readings as ground truth without verification.
Changing multiple environmental systems before confirming the measurement pattern.
content.practicalApplication: Create a room map with multiple temperature/RH measurement points at canopy level, upper canopy and return-air locations. Compare patterns through light-on, irrigation and light-off transitions.
content.summary: Advanced environmental control begins with trustworthy spatial measurement. Sensor maps reveal gradients that single-point control cannot see.
